did.unittitle: Raymond A. Crosby Stuyvesant Town collection
did.abstract: This collection, compiled by Raymond A. Crosby, the Renting Manager of Stuyvesant Town from 1946 to 1960, documents the early days of Stuyvesant Town, the largest private residential apartment community in the United States. Crosby saved photographs, memos, reports, floor plans, and dozens of letters written to him by prospective tenants desperate to move into Stuy Town.

arrangement.head: Arrangement
arrangement.p: This collection remains in the order in which it was donated and includes three folders: (1) biographical information about Raymond A. Crosby, (2) information about Raymond A. Crosby and Stuyvesant Town, and (3) letters to Raymond A. Crosby from prospective Stuyvesant Town tenants.

bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: Raymond Alexander Crosby (1895-1982) was born in Westfield, NJ and grew up in Brooklyn. He married Marie Elizabeth Mitchell in 1918; the couple had three children. After obtaining a position with the Housing Division of the Metropolitan Life Insurance Company at Parkchester in the Bronx in 1939, Crosby was transferred to the Stuyvesant Town development in Manhattan and appointed Renting Manager in 1946, a position he held until 1960. While working as Renting Manager, he married Helen Anna Sholes, a Stuy Town tenant, in 1949. The couple lived in Stuyvesant Town until moving to Pennsylvania in retirement. Crosby died in Palm Beach.

Stuyvesant Town and Peter Cooper Village were originally planned as a housing development during the early 1940s. The complex, developed by the Metropolitan Life Insurance Company, consists of 110 red brick apartment buildings on 80 acres between First Avenue and Avenue C and 14th Street and 23rd Street. Construction started in 1945, and the first completed building opened to tenants on August 1, 1947. In 1947, rents ranged from $50 to $91 per month. On the first day of its initial offering, the property received 7,000 applications; it would collect 100,000 applications by the time of first occupancy. The 11,250 apartments continued to be in high demand for the tenure of Crosby's employment.

processinfo.head: Processing Information
processinfo.p: The papers in this collection were originally in a black three-ring binder with cover title "Raymond A. Crosby, The Stuyvesant Town Years, 1939-1960." They were removed from the binder and placed in the original order in archival folders.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: The first folder contains biographical information about Raymond A. Crosby and his time at Stuyvesant Town. It includes a biographical sketch written in 2023 by John D. Crosby, Raymond A. Crosby's grandson; an autobiographical sketch written by Raymond A. Crosby, a newspaper clipping about Crosby's retirement as Renting Manager at Stuyvesant Town in 1960, and black & white photographs and photocopies of photographs of Crosby, his second wife Helen, and Stuyvesant Town.

The second folder covers Crosby's early years as Renting Manager at Stuyvesant Town and contains letters from friends and prospective tenants, flyers regarding staff changes at Stuyvesant Town, a report created by Crosby documenting "various statistical categories in relation to Stuyvesant Town tenancy" from 1960, a report giving details of the plannning and construction of Stuyvesant Town from the late 1940s, and numerous floor plans of apartments at Stuyvesant Town and Peter Cooper Village.

The third folder contains letters from prospective tenants hoping to rent an apartment at Stuyvesant Town. Almost all of the letters are from one couple, Charles and Marie Scimecca. Charles Scimecca was a graphic artist, and most of the letters include ink sketches with watercolor washes or collages.

did.unittitle: Biographical information about Raymond A. Crosby

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: This folder contains a brief biographical sketch of Raymond A. Crosby by his grandson, John D. Crosby, in which he explains his grandfather's position at the Stuyvesant Town housing complex in New York City. The sketch also contains photocopies of a black & white photograph of Crosby and his second wife, Helen, at Stuyvesant Town in 1947 and an undated photograph of Crosby holding a baby (ca. 1940s). There is also a photocopy of a three-page typed autobiography by Raymond Alexander Crosby from after 1949, photographs of Stuyvesant Town from the 1940s or 1950s, a photograph of Crosby and wife in Pennsylvania from 1969, and a clipping from Town & Village, New York, N.Y. from Thursday, December 29, 1960, documenting Crosby's retirement as Renting Manager at Stuyvesant Town.

did.unittitle: Information about Raymond A. Crosby and Stuyvesant Town

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p:
Folder includes the following:
• Typed poem about Bing Crosby from Christmas party, 1940, with attached clipping from Parkchester Press, 1941 January 2 (Raymond Crosby's friends called him Bing; he is not the singer Bing Crosby.)
• Autograph letter signed from Frank [no surname given] to Bing [Raymond A. Crosby], 1943 November 5, on stationery from Parklabrea, A Residential Community in Los Angeles. Frank refers to Crosby's "historical news," describes a dinner out with colleagues, and comments on his job renting model houses in California.
• Autograph letter signed from Mrs. Eleanor Ruesch to R.A. Crosby, Bayside, Queens, 1950 October 18, asking if he will have an apartment available to rent in Stuyvesant Town or Peter Cooper Village. With envelope with postmark.
• Autograph letter signed from Marjorie Wheelwright to Mr. Crosby, New York, 1952 January 14, thanking him for her lovely apartment and enclosing a nickel (taped to letter.)
• Typed letters and flyers concerning staff changes at Stuyvesant Town, 1955 May-June. The main staff change discussed is Arthur A. Wilson's replacement of Carl Huebner as Resident Manager of Stuyvesant Town.
• Typed report about Stuyvesant Town by R.A. Crosby, 1960 February 17. Report covers topics such as the number of apartments, size of families, population demographics, employment status and income level of tenants, families with children, overcrowded apartments, single occupants, etc. The report may be incomplete since later sections in the table of contents are not included.
• Report called "Stuyvesant Town," no author listed [possibly Crosby?], 1948 or later. The report provides details about the plan for Stuyvesant Town, the clearing of existing buildings and the Tenant Relocation Bureau, the housing development's construction, the high demand for the new apartments, the amenities and landscaping of the new development, the cost of apartments, the "plan in respect to taxes," and the names of the people involved in Stuyvesant Town's development.
• Floor plans for various apartment configurations at Stuyvesant Town and Peter Cooper Village, some with Crosby's notes on them, 1940s.

did.unittitle: Letters to Raymond A. Crosby from prospective Stuyvesant Town tenants

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: This folder includes letters written to Raymond Crosby by prospective tenants hoping he has an open apartment at Stuyvesant Town. One couple, Paul and Olga [Ollie] Calle, sent a few cards in 1952 October-November and a decorated Christmas card on 1952 December 9. All the remaining letters are from Charles and Marie Scimecca. They sent them frequently, even daily, during late 1948 and early 1949. More than fifty of these letters are included here, many of them with Crosby's added date to indicate when he received them.
